raw_response:
I am a woman of 29 years in Quzhou, but I have been on this land since before I can properly remember — my mother carried me on her back while she hoed, and by the time I was six I was pulling my own weight. I never went to school; the farm was my school. I know every corner of my 8 mu. Six mu I keep in the wheat-maize rotation that feeds us and brings steady money, and 2 mu I plant to cotton because when the price is good, cotton pays better than grain, though it costs more in labor and care.

My household has six mouths, and two of my brothers work in a factory in Handan, so they send money home but are not here for the busy seasons. That means I must plan the work so I can do most of it myself, with help only from my mother and father when they are able. We have our own well, so I do not fear drought like some, but pumping water costs electricity, and I am careful — I only irrigate when the crop truly needs it.

Right now it is early spring. My winter wheat went into the ground last October after rotary tillage. It is greening up. This spring I will spread urea at green-up and again at jointing — I have learned that two topdressings give me better grain than one heavy dose. I will irrigate three times: at jointing, at heading, and once more at grain-filling if May turns dry. I will spray herbicide once when the weeds first appear, and if I see aphids or powdery mildew, I will spray fungicide or insecticide once, no more. I use the same improved wheat seed my neighbors use — I save some seed, but I buy fresh every few years to keep vigor. I expect about 500 kg per mu from this wheat if the weather is kind.

After I cut the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize immediately on those same 6 mu. I will not till deeply — there is no time, and the stubble helps keep moisture. I plant hybrid maize, one package per mu. I put compound fertilizer in the seed furrow at planting, then side-dress urea at the big-trumpet stage. Summer rains usually help, but if July and August turn hot and dry, I will irrigate twice: once when the maize is jointing, and once during grain-filling. One herbicide spray at planting, and one insecticide spray if armyworms or borers show up. With good luck, that maize will yield about 600 kg per mu.

My 2 mu of cotton I will plough and prepare in late April, once the soil warms. I plant hybrid Bt cotton — the bollworm does less damage with these seeds, though I still must watch for aphids and spider mites. I lay plastic mulch to keep the soil warm and moist; it costs a bit for the film, but the seedlings come up stronger. For fertilizer, I spread compound as a base before planting, then topdress with more compound when flowering begins. Cotton is thirsty work: I irrigate three times, at seedling, flowering, and boll-setting. I spray three times for pests and once for weeds. It is more labor, but I expect about 260 kg of seed cotton per mu, and if the price holds at 3 yuan per half-kilo or better, that 2 mu will earn its keep.

I do not read books, but I read my fields. I watch the color of the wheat leaves, the tightness of the maize tassels, and the number of cotton bolls. I apply enough fertilizer to feed the crop but not so much that I waste money — my neighbors who pour on too much urea only grow taller weeds and thinner wallets.
